strengths: Well-motivated and clearly articulated problem formulation: generative modeling of dense trajectory grids from a single image, drawing a principled analogy to video generation architectures but avoiding pixel-space overhead.

Extensive and diverse experimental validation across multiple domains (Kubric, LIBERO, Physion, Physics101, real-world), including in-distribution and out-of-distribution splits, which strengthens generalizability claims.

Thoughtful evaluation methodology: introduces/adapts multiple complementary metrics (Best-of-K MSE, FVMD, FVMD(S), LRTL rigidity metric) that address different failure modes, along with sanity checks validating the metrics themselves (Table 21) and tracker reliability (Table 20).

Strong and convincing comparisons against a wide range of relevant baselines (ATM, Tra-MoE, Track2Act, MotionModes, and multiple fine-tuned large-scale video generators including WAN, SVD, DynamicCrafter, LTX), with fair-comparison efforts (e.g., filtering schemes favoring baselines, matched latent dimensionality ablation in Table 6).

The central hypothesis—that pixel generation overhead harms motion plausibility relative to direct trajectory modeling—is tested directly via a controlled modality-ablation experiment (Table 6) holding architecture, training time, and latent dimensionality fixed, which is a nice piece of causal-style evidence.
Includes a human user study corroborating the quantitative metrics, plus thorough reproducibility details (architecture diagrams, hyperparameters, compute budgets) in the appendix.
Useful ablations on model scale, latent space (VAE vs raw coordinates) with an interesting mode-collapse analysis (Figure 7/8), and pseudo-label vs ground-truth trajectory training.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is largely an adaptation/combination of existing components (flow matching, VAE latent space, DiT/Latte-style spatio-temporal transformer with cross-attention) applied to a new output modality (trajectories instead of pixels); the architectural novelty is incremental relative to prior video generators and trajectory diffusion methods like Track2Act.

The VAE ablation results are mixed and somewhat inconclusive on real data (Physics101, Table 14), where the method without VAE performs better overall, weakening the generality of the latent-space design justification presented as a main architectural choice.

Real-world quantitative evaluation is limited to a single sample per initial condition (no distributional metrics possible), and generalization to truly in-the-wild scenes (Physion→real transfer) is only assessed qualitatively due to small dataset size, limiting confidence in real-world applicability.

The user study is relatively small in scale (16 scenes, 20 users) and only compares against two video-generation baselines, not against the trajectory regression/generation baselines (ATM, Tra-MoE, Track2Act, MotionModes), which would have been a valuable addition given the paper's core claims.

Some comparisons could raise fairness concerns, e.g., regression baselines (ATM, Tra-MoE) are deterministic (k=1) while the proposed method benefits from sampling multiple hypotheses (k=8) and reporting Min/Mean-of-k, which inherently favors a stochastic generator on ambiguous tasks; while acknowledged, the practical implication (i.e., how would one select the correct hypothesis at deployment) is not fully addressed.

The claim that video generators fundamentally struggle due to 'pixel generation overhead' is supported mainly through comparisons on synthetic domains with relatively small/simple scenes; it remains unclear how well this conclusion holds for more complex, textured, real-world scenes where fine-tuned large video models might have more relative advantage.

Limited discussion of failure cases or scenarios where the proposed dense grid/trajectory approach might itself struggle (e.g., topology changes, non-rigid highly deformable objects, occlusion-heavy scenes), beyond what is included in the Limitations section.

strengths: Extensive experimental evaluation spanning multiple domains (Kubric, LIBERO, Physion, Physics101) covering both synthetic and real data, which is unusually broad for this type of work.

The core hypothesis that RGB-pixel generation overhead (rather than lack of capacity/scale) is responsible for poor motion plausibility in video generators is tested with a well-controlled ablation (Table 6) that fixes architecture and only varies the output modality (RGB latents of comparable dimensionality vs. trajectory latents) -- this is a genuinely useful empirical contribution for the 'world models' debate.

Thoughtful set of complementary evaluation metrics (Best-of-K MSE, FVMD, image-conditional FVMD(S), and a novel rigidity metric LRTL), along with a sanity check of these metrics (ground truth vs. ground truth, Table 21) and tracker reliability checks (Table 20).

Substantial ablation studies (VAE vs. raw coordinates, model scale, pseudo-label vs. ground-truth trajectory supervision) and a qualitative latent-interpolation analysis (Fig. 9) that helps explain why the latent space improves diversity/mode coverage (Fig. 7/8).
Reasonably strong reproducibility effort: detailed hyperparameters, compute budgets, and architecture diagrams are provided in the appendix.
Validation beyond automatic metrics via a human preference/ELO study, lending some real-world credibility to the quantitative claims.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is incremental: the model is essentially an existing video-diffusion-style architecture (Latte/DiT blocks, flow matching, VAE latent space, DINOv2 cross-attention) repurposed to output trajectory grids instead of pixels. No fundamentally new modeling techniques are introduced; the novelty is primarily in the application/output modality rather than in methodology.

Comparisons with large pretrained video generators (WAN 14B/1.3B, SVD, LTX, DynamicCrafter) are not entirely apples-to-apples: these models were fine-tuned for limited, possibly insufficient durations/compute relative to their scale, and it's unclear whether more extensive fine-tuning or scale-matched training would close the gap, weakening the strength of the 'pixel overhead' claim as a fully general conclusion about world models.

Real-world quantitative results (Physics101) are mixed and relatively weak evidence for the paper's central claims: the proposed method wins overall by a small margin (28.62 vs 30.08) and actually loses to WAN in 2 of 5 scenarios (Liquid, Ramp), undermining the strong framing in the abstract/intro that video generators 'struggle' broadly.

The VAE ablation, a key architectural choice, is not convincingly validated: Table 14 shows the model performs worse with the VAE on Physics101, which is inconsistent with the paper's stated preference for the latent formulation and is explained away somewhat post-hoc.
Generalization claims to real/in-the-wild scenes (Fig. 6, Physion transfer) remain purely qualitative with no quantitative metrics, limiting the strength of the generalization narrative.

Several baseline comparisons involve nontrivial re-engineering of the baselines (e.g., modifying Track2Act's conditioning, prediction horizon, and number of output points; applying custom filtering/sampling schemes for ATM/Tra-MoE), which, despite stated efforts at fairness, introduces potential bias and makes the comparisons harder to interpret as strictly faithful to original baseline performance.

The dense grid formulation, while framed as a key contribution, is a fairly natural extension of existing per-point/trajectory generation frameworks (e.g., CoTracker-style dense tracking, video generation grids) and the benefit over sparse trajectory baselines may stem largely from using more conditioning information/points rather than a fundamentally better formulation.

The paper's abstract and framing ('struggle... despite fine-tuning', 'this limitation arises from the overhead of generating pixels') are stated with more confidence than the mixed empirical evidence (especially on real data) fully supports.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly formulated problem: casting single-image motion forecasting as conditional generation of dense point trajectory grids using a flow-matching latent VAE architecture, closely mirroring modern video generators but avoiding pixel-space overhead.

Thorough and diverse experimental evaluation spanning multiple synthetic benchmarks (Kubric, LIBERO, Physion) and a real dataset (Physics101), with both in-distribution and out-of-distribution splits.

Strong and fair baselines comparisons: regression-based trajectory predictors (ATM, Tra-MoE), another generative trajectory baseline (Track2Act), training-free motion generators (MotionModes), and multiple state-of-the-art large-scale video generators (WAN, SVD, LTX, DynamicCrafter), including fine-tuned variants to control for domain gap.

Good metric design: introduces/adapts complementary metrics (Best-of-K MSE, FVMD/FVMD(S), LRTL rigidity metric) that capture different aspects (accuracy, distributional plausibility, physical plausibility), with sanity checks validating their usefulness (Table 21, CoTracker tracking accuracy check).

Includes a controlled ablation (Section 4.3, Table 6) isolating the effect of output modality (RGB vs trajectories) while holding architecture, latent dimensionality, and training budget fixed, providing convincing causal evidence for the central claim that trajectory generation outperforms pixel generation for motion forecasting.

Extensive reproducibility details and ablations in the appendix (model configs, training hyperparameters, VAE ablations, model scale ablations, latent space ablations, evaluation cost accounting), plus a human preference user study reinforcing the quantitative results.
Demonstrates some encouraging real-world generalization (Physion-trained model applied to real captured scenes) despite only synthetic training, and includes honest discussion of limitations.
weaknesses: The real-world Physics101 comparison is comparatively weak: only a single sample is drawn per method due to computational cost, undermining the core premise of the paper (multi-hypothesis generative modeling of uncertainty), and the head-to-head MSE results are mixed (our method wins overall but loses in 2/5 scenarios), with no distributional/rigidity metrics reported there due to lack of multiple ground truths.

Quantitative real-world generalization (Physion-to-real) is purely qualitative; the small real dataset size limits the strength of the generalization claims to real, unconstrained scenes beyond simulation.

The central claim that video generators are poor motion forecasters is demonstrated mainly on fairly simple/synthetic physical scenes (Kubric primitives, Physics101 lab scenarios); it remains unclear how well this generalizes to more complex, cluttered, or deformable real-world dynamics or longer horizons.

VAE ablation results are inconsistent across datasets (helps on Kubric/LIBERO, mixed/worse on Physics101), and the explanation offered (diversity vs. single ground truth evaluation) is somewhat post-hoc rather than rigorously tested.

Grid-based dense trajectory representation may not scale gracefully to higher resolutions or longer time horizons given its tensor size growth, and the paper does not deeply explore runtime/memory scaling trade-offs beyond the provided table for short clips.

The user study is relatively small (16 scenes, 20 users) and compares against only two video generator baselines (SVD, WAN 1.3B), not the larger WAN 14B or other strong baselines shown in Table 3, limiting generality of the subjective evaluation.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated formulation of single-image motion forecasting as conditional generation of dense point trajectory grids using flow matching, adapting video-generator architectures (DiT/Latte-style spatio-temporal transformer with cross-attention to image tokens) to the trajectory modality.

Extensive experimental evaluation across multiple domains: LIBERO robotics data, synthetic Kubric (in- and out-of-distribution), Physion, and two real-world datasets (Physics101, Cityscapes), plus a real-world qualitative generalization study.

Thoughtful and diverse evaluation protocol combining Best-of-K MSE, distributional metrics (FVMD/FVMD(S)), and a novel rigidity-based metric (LRTL) that captures physical plausibility beyond simple distributional similarity, along with sanity checks validating the metrics.

The core hypothesis -- that RGB generation overhead harms motion quality relative to directly modeling trajectories -- is tested via a well-controlled ablation (Section 4.3) holding architecture and latent dimensionality fixed while swapping modality, which is a convincing and interesting empirical contribution.

Comprehensive comparisons against multiple relevant baselines (ATM, Tra-MoE, Track2Act, MotionModes, several fine-tuned video generators including WAN, SVD, LTX, DynamicCrafter) with consistent improvements reported across most settings.

Thorough appendix with ablations on model scale, VAE necessity, sampling density, multi-frame conditioning extension, and detailed reproducibility information (hyperparameters, compute cost, protocols).
weaknesses: Physics101 results (Table 8) are mixed -- the proposed method underperforms WAN in 2/5 scenarios (Fall, Liquid) and only modestly outperforms overall, which somewhat undercuts the paper's strong overarching claim that trajectory generation is uniformly superior to RGB video generation for motion forecasting.

Real-world evaluation is comparatively weak: Physics101 and Cityscapes reported metrics rely on pseudo-ground-truth trajectories extracted via CoTracker3 rather than true ground truth, and the Physion real-world generalization study is purely qualitative with no quantitative metrics, limiting the strength of claims about real-world applicability.

The user study is small in scale (16 scenes, 20 users) and compares only against two baselines (SVD, WAN 1.3B), not against Track2Act or the regression baselines, and margins (52% vs ~48% combined for two competitors) are relatively modest despite being framed as a clear win.

Some comparisons may not be fully apples-to-apples: e.g., video generator baselines require an extra point-tracking step (CoTracker3) to extract trajectories, which introduces its own error source, and it's not entirely clear whether compute/data budgets (e.g., fine-tuning duration matched to training time of the proposed model rather than to convergence) are fair to the large pretrained video models, especially given their vastly larger parameter counts and different training data distributions.

The VAE ablation (Table 16) shows the method actually performs worse with the VAE on Physics101 real data, which is a notable inconsistency with the paper's general narrative that latent modeling is beneficial, and this discrepancy is only briefly acknowledged rather than deeply analyzed.

The paper's central efficiency argument (motion modeling without pixel generation overhead) is somewhat expected/intuitive given that trajectory representations are inherently lower-dimensional and object-centric; the novelty is more in careful engineering and evaluation than in fundamentally new methodology, since the core techniques (flow matching, VAE latents, DiT-style architecture with cross-attention) are directly adapted from existing video generation frameworks.

Grid-based dense trajectory prediction may struggle to scale to more complex, cluttered, or higher-resolution real scenes beyond the relatively controlled/simple synthetic scenarios tested, and the paper's own limitations section acknowledges boundary-accuracy issues and limited in-the-wild generalization, which somewhat tempers the significance of the claimed contributions.

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation spanning multiple synthetic benchmarks (Kubric, LIBERO, Physion) and real-world data (Physics101, Cityscapes), with comparisons against a wide range of baselines (ATM, Tra-MoE, Track2Act, MotionModes, and several large video generators including WAN, SVD, LTX-Video, DynamicCrafter).

The core empirical claim -- that directly generating point trajectories avoids the 'pixel overhead' that hampers video generators at modeling motion -- is interesting and is supported by a reasonably controlled ablation (Table 6) that fixes the backbone architecture and only swaps output modality.

Good set of complementary metrics (Best-of-K MSE, FVMD/FVMD(S), and a rigidity-based LRTL metric) that attempt to capture different failure modes (diversity, distributional match, physical plausibility), going beyond simple regression error used by prior trajectory-forecasting works.
Reasonably thorough ablation study (model size, VAE vs. raw coordinates, sampling density, trajectory source) and inclusion of a user study for qualitative validation.
Clear and detailed reproducibility documentation (architecture diagrams, hyperparameters, compute budgets) in the appendix.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is limited: the method is essentially a direct transplant of an existing video-generation recipe (Latte/DiT-style spatio-temporal transformer + VAE + rectified flow, as used in WAN/MovieGen/LTX) onto a trajectory grid, with image conditioning via DINOv2 cross-attention. Nearly every individual component (VAE, flow matching, spatio-temporal factorized attention, QK-norm, gated cross-attention) is borrowed wholesale from prior work; the contribution is primarily an application/engineering combination rather than a new modeling idea.

The central comparison between the proposed trajectory generator and large pretrained video generators is confounded: the video baselines are much larger, pretrained on vastly different and more general data distributions, and are only given a fixed fine-tuning budget matched to the trajectory model's training time rather than matched in a way that controls for architecture capacity, pretraining exposure, or inference-time compute. This makes the central claim ('pixel generation overhead causes implausible motion, not lack of data/capacity') only partially supported -- it is plausible the gap is instead due to domain mismatch or insufficient fine-tuning of billion-parameter models on a tiny synthetic dataset.

Evaluation design has several fairness/validity concerns: on Physics101 and Cityscapes only a single sample is drawn per baseline and compared against a single pseudo ground truth obtained via CoTracker3, which is also the pseudo-labeling scheme used to train the proposed model, likely biasing results in favor of the trajectory-based approach whose supervision signal and evaluation protocol are self-consistent. Likewise, Track2Act is substantially modified (goal frame dropped, point count changed, horizon extended) in ways not clearly shown to be neutral.

Internal consistency of ablations is weak: the VAE latent-space ablation (Section B) shows contradictory effects across datasets (Table 15 vs. Table 16), undermining the strength of the claimed benefit of latent flow matching, and the paper acknowledges this without fully resolving it.

The proposed LRTL and FVMD(S) metrics are novel but only lightly validated (a single sanity check in Table 24); it is unclear how sensitive conclusions are to these specific metric choices, and no inter-metric correlation with human judgment (beyond a small 16-scene user study) is reported.

The real-world generalization evidence (Physion-to-real, Cityscapes) is largely qualitative or based on very small test sets, limiting confidence that the method generalizes beyond narrow synthetic domains despite the paper's broader framing as addressing general motion forecasting/world-model limitations.

Presentation is dense and the core contribution claim ('what happens next') is somewhat oversold relative to the actual scope, which is largely restricted to simple rigid-body/synthetic physical scenarios and short horizons (16-30 frames).

strengths: Novel and well-motivated reformulation of single-image motion forecasting as conditional generation of dense point-trajectory grids via latent flow matching, closely mirroring modern video-generator architectures but applied to a more tractable output modality.

Very thorough empirical evaluation spanning multiple synthetic domains (Kubric in- and out-of-distribution, LIBERO, Physion) and real-world data (Physics101, Cityscapes), with consistent gains over both regression-based trajectory predictors (ATM, Tra-MoE) and generative baselines (Track2Act, MotionModes) as well as large pretrained/fine-tuned video generators (WAN, SVD, LTX, DynamicCrafter).

The modality ablation (Section 4.3/Table 6), which fixes the architecture and only swaps RGB vs. trajectory latents (and tests a joint RGB+track model), is a particularly compelling and well-controlled experiment that directly supports the central claim that pixel-generation overhead hurts motion plausibility.

Good methodological care in evaluation: multiple complementary metrics (Best-of-K MSE, FVMD/FVMD(S), LRTL rigidity score) with a sanity check validating that these metrics behave sensibly (Table 24), plus a human preference study that corroborates the automatic metrics.

Extensive ablations on model scale, VAE vs. raw coordinate generation, sampling density, and multi-frame conditioning, together with substantial reproducibility details (hyperparameters, compute budgets, architecture diagrams) in the appendix.

Fair baseline treatment is explicitly discussed (e.g., favoring baselines by using their point-filtering schemes, equalizing training time/compute for finetuned video models), which strengthens the credibility of the comparisons.
weaknesses: Real-world evaluation is comparatively weak: Physics101 results use only a single sample per initial condition due to sampling cost from video generators, undermining the ability to assess the stochastic/diversity claims that are central to the paper's motivation on real data, and Cityscapes/Physics101 rely on CoTracker pseudo-labels for both training and evaluation, which introduces some circularity and potential label noise shared across methods.

The paper does not evaluate downstream task utility (e.g., policy success rates as in ATM/Tra-MoE), only trajectory-quality proxy metrics; it would strengthen the significance claim to show that improved trajectory generation actually improves robotic manipulation or planning performance.

Comparisons to some baselines (e.g., Track2Act) involve notable modifications (dropping goal-frame conditioning, extended prediction horizon, fixed point count) that, while argued to be fair, make the comparison less a faithful reproduction of the original method and could be seen as advantaging the proposed approach.

Several introduced physical-plausibility metrics (LRTL, FVMD(S)) are somewhat ad hoc; although a sanity check is provided, deeper validation against human judgments of rigidity/plausibility (beyond the overall ranking user study) would make the metrics more convincing.

The video-generator baselines are relatively small-to-mid scale for feasible fine-tuning (e.g., WAN 1.3B primarily, WAN 14B only evaluated zero-shot), so claims about limitations of "state-of-the-art video generators as world models" may not fully generalize to the largest current models.

Limited analysis of failure cases or boundary conditions of the proposed method itself (e.g., performance degradation with complex scenes, many interacting objects, or long horizons) beyond the brief out-of-distribution Kubric test.
